\chapter{-ncia --- Turning a Quality into a Thing}
\label{ch:ncia}
\hlchaptermodality{62}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can read an -ncia word as English -nce, know it is feminine, and describe it.}

Read preferencia, choose la for distancia, and say una diferencia grande.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[-ncia]{-ncia}

\label{lesson:ES-C09-ncia}



\begin{quote}
\emph{-oso} in English? (\emph{\textbf{-ous}}.) And \emph{-ción}? (\emph{\textbf{-tion}}.)

One more, and it is the one that makes ideas into things.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: a quality, made into a thing}]
\begin{quote}
\textbf{Spanish \emph{-ncia} is English \emph{-nce}.}
\end{quote}

Latin \textbf{-entia} turned a quality into a noun. If something \emph{differs}, the state of differing is \emph{differentia}. Spanish kept the ending nearly whole; English took it through French, where it wore down to \emph{-nce}.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Spanish} & \textbf{English} \\
\midrule
\emph{diferencia} & \textbf{difference} \\
\emph{importancia} & \textbf{importance} \\
\emph{experiencia} & \textbf{experience} \\
\emph{distancia} & \textbf{distance} \\
\emph{paciencia} & \textbf{patience} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

One word wearing two coats, five times over. This is the same shape as \emph{-ción} and \emph{-tion}: not a resemblance, the \textbf{same ending} arriving by two roads.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: what you do with it}]
Every \emph{-ncia} word is a \textbf{noun}, and every one is \textbf{feminine} — so the article never surprises you:

\begin{quote}
\emph{la diferencia}  ·  \emph{la importancia}  ·  \emph{una experiencia}
\end{quote}

And you already know what goes after a noun:

\begin{quote}
\emph{una diferencia \textbf{grande}} — a big difference
\end{quote}

That sentence uses three things you were taught separately: a noun built by an ending, an article chosen by gender, and a describing word in its Spanish position. None of it was memorised as a phrase.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{culture}
\textbf{One that will look wrong, and is not.}

\emph{Ciencia} is \textbf{science}, not \emph{cience}. The ending behaved exactly as promised — it is the \emph{root} that English spells differently, because \emph{scientia} came into English through a French spelling that kept the \emph{sc-}.

So when a decoded word looks almost right, trust the ending and check the root. Almost right is usually right.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{la diferencia, la importancia, la experiencia}
  \item \emph{una diferencia grande}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
\emph{-ncia} in English? (\emph{\textbf{-nce}}.) What gender, always? (\textbf{Feminine}.)

And when a decoded word looks \emph{almost} right? (Trust the ending, \textbf{check the root}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
